newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Strikes erupt again in S.Korea as showdown looms.
newsitem.headline: Strikes erupt again in S.Korea as showdown looms.

text.p: Labour strikes flared again in South Korea with renewed militancy on Monday after prosecutors summoned top union leaders for questioning, setting up a showdown between the government and workers.
Almost 150,000 workers walked out, including some 100,000 at the giant Daewoo and Hyundai groups, as all-out industrial war loomed over a new labour bill.
Car production was paralysed and two of the country's biggest shipyards were idled.
Senior prosecutor Lee Sang-hyong said about 20 leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions were ordered to appear before prosecutors by Tuesday.
The president of the confederation, Kwon Young-kil, dismissed the prosecution move and threatened to extend strikes that the government has declared unlawful.
"We will not respond to the prosecution summons," Kwon told a news conference.
He added that no summons had yet been delivered to union leaders, many of them huddling in a makeshift tent pitched on the snow-covered grounds of Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral in sub-zero conditions.

Kwon said workers at hospitals, broadcasters and medical insurance firms would join the stoppages unless President Kim Young-sam announced a repeal of the controversial labour bill at a news conference scheduled for Tuesday.

The law, rammed through parliament on December 26, allows employers to lay off workers, eroding decades of near-total job security. It also enables companies to replace strikers and hire temporary workers.
Kwon accused the government of trying to divert public attention from the industrial unrest by provoking a showdown between unions and public prosecutors.
"Despite the government's strong response we will push on with our strikes and we won't back down," Kwon said.

Hyundai Motor Co and 12 other Hyundai Group affiliates, including Hyundai Mipo Dockyard Co, began an indefinite strike affecting 73,341 union workers, a union official said. Hyundai Group has 20 unions in total.

Daewoo Motor Co, Daewoo Heavy Industries Ltd -- which operates the group's shipyard -- and four other Daewoo Group units were also idled after 27,650 unionised workers walked out, union officials said.
Production lines at Kia Motors were also at a standstill as 18,000 workers continued strike action.
Ssangyong Motor Co's 7,853 union workers voted to resume their walkout.

White-collar workers at government-backed research institutes and industry associations joined in under the banner of the Korea Federation of Professional and Technicians Unions that represents 14,256 staff.

In a sign of an imminent crackdown, police stepped up surveillance of labour protests on Sunday in Seoul. Uniformed police checked the identification papers of demonstrators and plainclothes officers took notes as labour leaders made speeches denouncing the government.
Prosecutor Lee said about 10 confederation leaders must report to the Seoul Prosecution Office and the others to local prosecutors responsible for provincial areas.
Stocks fell from the opening bell on news of the crackdown and fears that action against union leaders would further inflame industrial unrest.
"Worries that the strikes will intensify is really hurting sentiment," said broker Ha Young-hyun of Hyundai Securities. "I don't see much room for improvement at the moment."
